Handoff — od chat item-a do stvarnog rada (implementirano ✓) Nastalo posle korisnikovog uživo korišćenja: „ne zna se gde handoff ide", i „novi milestone se kreirao bez ikakvog odobrenja klijenta, a to znači nove sate i cenu". ### Tvrdo ograničenje modela (provereno u kodu, nije pretpostavka) `models/ProjectProposal.js` ima **unique indeks `{ projectId, phaseNumber }`** → **jedna ponuda po fazi**. Posledica: prihvaćena faza **ne može** dobiti još jedan milestone kroz odobrenje, jer bi to zahtevalo drugu ponudu za isti `phaseNumber`. Zato: > **Svaki novi rad koji traži odobrenje postaje NOVA faza.** Ne postoji „dodaj milestone u postojeću fazu uz Send" — arhitektura to ne dozvoljava bez migracije. Korisnik je to prihvatio kao odluku. ### Tri ishoda, razlika je komercijalna a ne tehnička | Ishod | Odobrenje | Endpoint | |---|---|---| | Task u **prihvaćen** milestone | ne treba — u dogovorenom obimu, primenjuje se odmah | `POST /api/project-items/:id/task` | | **Nov rad** (milestone i/ili faza) | **da** — draft ponuda → Send → klijent prihvata → `reconcileProposalMilestones` materijalizuje | `POST /api/project-items/:id/handoff` | | Povlačenje / brisanje | — | `POST .../proposals/:pid/withdraw` (sent→draft), `DELETE .../proposals/:pid` (samo draft/rejected) | **Uklonjeno:** `POST /api/project-items/:id/milestone` — pisalo je živ milestone bez odobrenja. Zabeleženo kao ispravka. ### Vidljivost - `PendingWorkSection` (admin, vrh kartice projekta): sve u `draft|sent|changes_requested|rejected`, status rečima („Awaiting client · 2d"), poreklo `D-001` preko `sourceItemRef`, akcije Edit/Send/Withdraw/Delete. Prihvaćeno se ne prikazuje — to je već u stablu. - **Admin stablo grupisano po fazama** (`(phaseNumber, order)` + separator). Ranije samo po `order`, a `order` je faza-lokalan → faze su se preplitale. - `ProjectItem.handoffProposalId` / `ProjectProposal.sourceItemId`+`sourceItemRef` drže vezu u oba smera. --- ## 13A-2. Brisanje ponuda — pun životni ciklus (implementirano ✓) Ranije nije bilo dokumentovano, a u praksi je bio ćorsokak. Pravilo: **meko pa tvrdo** — ništa se ne briše iz baze dok prvo ne bude odmotano iz plana. ``` draft ─────────────────────────────────────▶ Delete forever sent ──── Withdraw ──▶ draft ──────────────▶ Delete forever rejected ──────────────────────────────────▶ Delete forever accepted ─ Delete phase (arhivira) ─▶ archived ─▶ Delete forever master (faza 1) ───────────────────────────▶ NIKAD (zaštićen) ``` - **„Delete phase"** = meko: `status → archived`, milestone-ovi se `$pull`-uju iz projekta u transakciji, zapis ostaje sa razlogom (`archiveReason`) i događajem u feed-u. - **„Delete forever"** = tvrdo: briše red iz baze, čisti `archivedProposalIds` i `handoffProposalId`. Ne nudi se za `sent`/`accepted` — tamo prvo ide withdraw odnosno archive. ### Operatorski override nad započetim radom Do sada je `preparePhaseArchive` bezuslovno odbijao arhiviranje ako je bilo šta u fazi započeto (`workStartedAt`, status ≠ `pending`, započet task, ili postojeći `changeHistory`) — dugme je bilo **disabled** i faza je ostajala neuklonjiva zauvek. To je bila namerna politika („dogovoren i započet rad je trajan zapis"), ali je pravila ćorsokak kad admin uoči sopstvenu grešku ili se sa klijentom naknadno dogovori da se deo izbaci. Nova politika (potvrdio korisnik): **admin sme da ukloni i započetu prihvaćenu fazu, bez odobrenja klijenta**, ali: - `preparePhaseArchive(proposal, milestones, { force: true })` — `force` **ne proširuje ŠTA** sme da se obriše: master proposal i ne-`accepted` statusi i dalje bacaju `MASTER_PROPOSAL_IMMUTABLE` / `PHASE_NOT_ACCEPTED`. tools.name: get_vscode_api
tools.description:
Get comprehensive VS Code API documentation and references for extension development. This tool provides authoritative documentation for VS Code's extensive API surface, including proposed APIs, contribution points, and best practices. Use this tool for understanding complex VS Code API interactions.

When to use this tool:
- User asks about specific VS Code APIs, interfaces, or extension capabilities
- Need documentation for VS Code extension contribution points (commands, views, settings, etc.)
- Questions about proposed APIs and their usage patterns
- Understanding VS Code extension lifecycle, activation events, and packaging
- Best practices for VS Code extension development architecture
- API examples and code patterns for extension features
- Troubleshooting extension-specific issues or API limitations

When NOT to use this tool:
- Creating simple standalone files or scripts unrelated to VS Code extensions
- General programming questions not specific to VS Code extension development
- Questions about using VS Code as an editor (user-facing features)
- Non-extension related development tasks
- File creation or editing that doesn't involve VS Code extension APIs

CRITICAL usage guidelines:
1. Always include specific API names, interfaces, or concepts in your query
2. Mention the extension feature you're trying to implement
3. Include context about proposed vs stable APIs when relevant
4. Reference specific contribution points when asking about extension manifest
5. Be specific about the VS Code version or API version when known

Scope: This tool is for EXTENSION DEVELOPMENT ONLY - building tools that extend VS Code itself, not for general file creation or non-extension programming tasks.

query.description: The query to search vscode documentation for. Should contain all relevant context.

tools.name: memory
tools.description:
Manage a persistent memory system with three scopes for storing notes and information across conversations.

Memory is organized under /memories/ with three tiers:
- `/memories/` — User memory: persistent notes that survive across all workspaces and conversations. Store preferences, patterns, and general insights here.
- `/memories/session/` — Session memory: notes scoped to the current conversation. Store task-specific context and in-progress notes here. Cleared after the conversation ends.
- `/memories/repo/` — Repository memory: repository-scoped notes stored locally in the workspace. Store codebase conventions, build commands, project structure facts, and verified practices here.

IMPORTANT: Before creating new memory files, first view the /memories/ directory to understand what already exists. This helps avoid duplicates and maintain organized notes.

Commands:
- `view`: View contents of a file or list directory contents. Can be used on files or directories (e.g., "/memories/" to see all top-level items).
- `create`: Create a new file at the specified path with the given content. Fails if the file already exists.
- `str_replace`: Replace an exact string in a file with a new string. The old_str must appear exactly once in the file.
- `insert`: Insert text at a specific line number in a file. Line 0 inserts at the beginning.
- `delete`: Delete a file or directory (and all its contents).
- `rename`: Rename or move a file or directory from path to new_path. Cannot rename across scopes.

command.description: The operation to perform on the memory file system.

path.description: The absolute path to the file or directory inside /memories/, e.g. "/memories/notes.md". Used by all commands except `rename`.

file_text.description: Required for `create`. The content of the file to create.

old_str.description: Required for `str_replace`. The exact string in the file to replace. Must appear exactly once.

new_str.description: Required for `str_replace`. The new string to replace old_str with.

insert_line.description: Required for `insert`. The 0-based line number to insert text at. 0 inserts before the first line.

insert_text.description: Required for `insert`. The text to insert at the specified line.

view_range.description: Optional for `view`. A two-element array [start_line, end_line] (1-indexed) to view a specific range of lines.

old_path.description: Required for `rename`. The current path of the file or directory to rename.

new_path.description: Required for `rename`. The new path for the file or directory.

Prefer reading larger ranges over doing many small reads. Binary files use startLine/endLine as byte offsets.

tools.name: replace_string_in_file
tools.description:
This is a tool for making edits in an existing file in the workspace. For moving or renaming files, use run in terminal tool with the 'mv' command instead. For larger edits, split them into smaller edits and call the edit tool multiple times to ensure accuracy. Before editing, always ensure you have the context to understand the file's contents and context. To edit a file, provide: 1) filePath (absolute path), 2) oldString (MUST be the exact literal text to replace including all whitespace, indentation, newlines, and surrounding code etc), and 3) newString (MUST be the exact literal text to replace \`oldString\` with (also including all whitespace, indentation, newlines, and surrounding code etc.). Ensure the resulting code is correct and idiomatic.). Each use of this tool replaces exactly ONE occurrence of oldString.

CRITICAL for \`oldString\`: Must uniquely identify the single instance to change. Include at least 3 lines of context BEFORE and AFTER the target text, matching whitespace and indentation precisely. If this string matches multiple locations, or does not match exactly, the tool will fail. Never use 'Lines 123-456 omitted' from summarized documents or ...existing code... comments in the oldString or newString.

filePath.description: An absolute path to the file to edit.

oldString.description: The exact literal text to replace, preferably unescaped. For single replacements (default), include at least 3 lines of context BEFORE and AFTER the target text, matching whitespace and indentation precisely. For multiple replacements, specify expected_replacements parameter. If this string is not the exact literal text (i.e. you escaped it) or does not match exactly, the tool will fail.

newString.description: The exact literal text to replace `old_string` with, preferably unescaped. Provide the EXACT text. Ensure the resulting code is correct and idiomatic.

Code cells are ready to run and don't require any pre-processing. If asked to run the first cell in a notebook, you should run the first code cell since markdown cells cannot be executed. NOTE: Avoid executing Markdown cells or providing Markdown cell IDs, as Markdown cells cannot be  executed.

tools.name: session_store_sql
tools.description:
Query the local session store containing history from past coding sessions. Uses SQLite syntax (NOT DuckDB or Postgres). SQL queries are read-only — only SELECT and WITH are allowed. Use `datetime('now', '-1 day')` for date math (NOT `now() - INTERVAL '1 day'`), FTS5 `MATCH` for text search.

Tables: `sessions`, `turns`, `session_files`, `session_refs`, `checkpoints`, `search_index`. For column details and query patterns, use the **chronicle** skill.

tools.name: vscode_listCodeUsages
tools.description:
Find all usages (references, definitions, and implementations) of a code symbol across the workspace. This tool locates where a symbol is referenced, defined, or implemented.

Input:
- "symbol": The exact name of the symbol to search for (function, class, method, variable, type, etc.).
- "uri": A full URI (e.g. "file:///path/to/file.ts") of a file where the symbol appears. Provide either "uri" or "filePath".
- "filePath": A workspace-relative file path (e.g. "src/utils/helpers.ts") of a file where the symbol appears. Provide either "uri" or "filePath".
- "lineContent": A substring of the line of code where the symbol appears. This is used to locate the exact position in the file. Must be the actual text from the file - do NOT fabricate it.

IMPORTANT: The file and line do NOT need to be the definition of the symbol. Any occurrence works - a usage, an import, a call site, etc. You can pick whichever occurrence is most convenient.

If the tool returns an error, retry with corrected input - ensure the file path is correct, the line content matches the actual file content, and the symbol name appears in that line.

If the file's language has no reference provider registered, the tool returns an error.

tools.name: manage_todo_list
tools.description:
Manage a structured todo list to track progress and plan tasks throughout your coding session. Use this tool VERY frequently to ensure task visibility and proper planning.

When to use this tool:
- Complex multi-step work requiring planning and tracking
- When user provides multiple tasks or requests (numbered/comma-separated)
- After receiving new instructions that require multiple steps
- BEFORE starting work on any todo (mark as in-progress)
- IMMEDIATELY after completing each todo (mark completed individually)
- When breaking down larger tasks into smaller actionable steps
- To give users visibility into your progress and planning

When NOT to use:
- Single, trivial tasks that can be completed in one step
- Purely conversational/informational requests
- When just reading files or performing simple searches

CRITICAL workflow:
1. Plan tasks by writing todo list with specific, actionable items
2. Mark ONE todo as in-progress before starting work
3. Complete the work for that specific todo
4. Mark that todo as completed IMMEDIATELY
5. Move to next todo and repeat

Todo states:
- not-started: Todo not yet begun
- in-progress: Currently working (limit ONE at a time)
- completed: Finished successfully

IMPORTANT: Mark todos completed as soon as they are done. Do not batch completions.

tools.name: run_in_terminal
tools.description:
This tool allows you to execute shell commands in a persistent bash terminal session, preserving environment variables, working directory, and other context across multiple commands.

Command Execution:
- Use && to chain simple commands on one line
- Prefer pipelines | over temporary files for data flow
- Never create a sub-shell (eg. bash -c "command") unless explicitly asked

Directory Management:
- Prefer relative paths when navigating directories, only use absolute when the path is far away or the current cwd is not expected
- By default (mode=sync), shell and cwd are reused by subsequent sync commands
- Use $PWD for current directory references
- Consider using pushd/popd for directory stack management
- Supports directory shortcuts like ~ and -

Program Execution:
- Supports Python, Node.js, and other executables
- Install packages via package managers (brew, apt, etc.)
- Use which or command -v to verify command availability

Execution Mode:
- For ALL one-shot commands (builds, tests, installs, compilation, linting, downloads, scripts), use mode='sync' and omit timeout. The tool waits for the command to complete and returns full output inline. This is the default and strongly preferred mode.
- Use mode='async' ONLY for processes that must keep running indefinitely while you do other work (servers, watchers, dev daemons). Async waits for an initial idle/output signal, then returns a terminal ID and output snapshot while the process continues running.
- In sync mode, the full output is returned when the command completes — you do NOT need to call get_terminal_output afterward. Only use get_terminal_output if the tool result explicitly says the command was moved to background, timed out, or needs input.

Use send_to_terminal to send commands or input to a terminal session.

Output Management:
- Output exceeding 20KB is saved to a temp file; the result includes the file path so you can read the full output with readFile or search it with grep
- Use head, tail, grep, awk to filter and limit output size
- For pager commands, disable paging: git --no-pager or add | cat
- Use wc -l to count lines before displaying large outputs

Best Practices:
- Quote variables: "$var" instead of $var to handle spaces
- Use find with -exec or xargs for file operations
- Be specific with commands to avoid excessive output
- Avoid printing credentials unless absolutely required
- Avoid commands that require interactive privilege escalation, such as sudo/su/doas without a non-interactive flag (e.g. sudo -n). They block on a password prompt that cannot be answered in this mode, and secrets must never be routed through the model. If a command needs elevated privileges, tell the user to run it themselves in the terminal and stop — do NOT retry the command with variations.
- NEVER run sleep or similar wait commands in a terminal. You will be automatically notified on your next turn when async terminal commands or timed-out sync commands complete or need input. Do NOT poll for completion.
- NEVER pipe interactive commands through tail, head, grep, or other filters — this hides prompts and prevents the terminal from detecting when input is needed. Run interactive commands without pipes.

Interactive Input Handling:
- When a terminal command is waiting for interactive input, do NOT suggest alternatives or ask the user whether to proceed. Instead, use the vscode_askQuestions tool to collect the needed values from the user, then send them.
- NEVER use vscode_askQuestions to request sensitive input such as passwords, passphrases, API keys, tokens, or other secrets — answers to that tool are sent through the model. If the prompt requires a secret, tell the user to type it directly into the terminal and stop; do not call vscode_askQuestions or send_to_terminal for that prompt.
- Send exactly one answer per prompt using send_to_terminal. Never send multiple answers in a single send.
- After each send, call get_terminal_output to read the next prompt before sending the next answer.
- Continue one prompt at a time until the command finishes.
- Use [[ ]] for conditional tests instead of [ ]
- Prefer $() over backticks for command substitution

Execution mode:
- mode='sync' (strongly preferred): waits for the command to complete and returns full output inline. Use for ALL one-shot commands (builds, tests, installs, compilation, scripts). Omit timeout to let the command run to completion — the tool handles idle detection and input prompts automatically.
- mode='async': waits for an initial idle/output signal from the command, then returns a terminal ID and output snapshot while the process continues running. Use ONLY for processes that must keep running indefinitely (servers, watchers, daemons). Timeout caps how long to wait for the initial idle/output signal.

Timeout parameter: Usually omit timeout entirely for sync commands — the tool returns automatically on completion, input-needed, or cancellation. Only set a timeout as a safety net for commands you suspect might hang. Use 0 to explicitly indicate no timeout.

Sync output is final: When a sync command completes, the full output is returned inline — do NOT call get_terminal_output afterward. Only use get_terminal_output if the tool result explicitly indicates the command was moved to background, timed out, or needs input. Do NOT tell the user to check the terminal panel — all command output is already included in the tool result.

Terminal notifications: When an async command finishes or a sync command times out, you will be automatically notified on your next turn with the exit code and terminal output. You will also be notified if the terminal needs input. Do NOT poll or sleep to wait for completion.

goal.description: A short description of the goal or purpose of the command (e.g., "Install dependencies", "Start development server").

Wait for an initial idle/output signal, then return a terminal ID and output snapshot while the process continues running. Timeout caps how long to wait for the initial signal. Use ONLY for processes that must keep running indefinitely (servers, watchers, daemons).

Only set a timeout (in milliseconds) as a safety net if you suspect the command might hang. If the timeout elapses, the command continues in the background and you get a terminal ID to check output later. Use 0 to explicitly indicate no timeout.

tools.name: runSubagent
tools.description:
Launch a new agent to handle complex, multi-step tasks autonomously. This tool is good at researching complex questions, searching for code, and executing multi-step tasks. When you are searching for a keyword or file and are not confident that you will find the right match in the first few tries, use this agent to perform the search for you.

- Agents do not run async or in the background, you will wait for the agent's result.
- When the agent is done, it will return a single message back to you. The result returned by the agent is not visible to the user. To show the user the result, you should send a text message back to the user with a concise summary of the result.
- Each agent invocation is stateless. You will not be able to send additional messages to the agent, nor will the agent be able to communicate with you outside of its final report. Therefore, your prompt should contain a highly detailed task description for the agent to perform autonomously and you should specify exactly what information the agent should return back to you in its final and only message to you.
- The agent's outputs should generally be trusted
- Clearly tell the agent whether you expect it to write code or just to do research (search, file reads, web fetches, etc.), since it is not aware of the user's intent
- If the user asks for a certain agent, you MUST provide that EXACT agent name (case-sensitive) to invoke that specific agent.

tools.name: mcp_pylance_mcp_s_pylanceAnalyze
tools.description: Pylance code-flow analysis for Python. One tool that dispatches between commands for tracing, typing, and visualizing program state. Commands: "traceValue" — walk the program flow graph backwards from a position to explain how a variable got its value (assignments, narrowing, try/except). Use when the user asks "where does this value come from?" or "what does this depend on?". "typeAt" — get the inferred/narrowed Python type at a position (lighter than `pylanceLSP textDocument/hover`, returns only the type). "flowGraph" — return an ASCII visualization of the code-flow graph at a position; useful for debugging unexpected narrowing or branch behavior. "traceFailure" — trace value provenance across multiple stack frames (caller-supplied, innermost-first); bridges through function-parameter boundaries by resolving the matching argument at each call site. "tracePytestFailure" — paste raw pytest failure output and the tool extracts frames, assertions, and variables automatically and runs traceFailure for each failure. "help" — full per-command parameter reference. Prefer `pylanceLSP textDocument/definition` for "where is this defined?"; use this tool for value provenance across reassignments and conditions, not symbol resolution. Positions are LSP 0-based `{ line, character }`; URIs must be `file://` and inside the workspace.

workspaceRoot.description: Optional workspace root for this tool call. Standalone MCP uses this before the server --workspace argument.

command.description: Analysis command to run. Use "help" for full per-command documentation, parameters, and examples.

fileUri.description: LSP file URI (e.g. "file:///workspace/foo.py") or absolute path. Required for traceValue, typeAt, flowGraph.

position.description: LSP-style 0-based position. Required for traceValue, typeAt, flowGraph.

symbol.description: Variable/symbol name to trace. Required for traceValue.

transitive.description: For traceValue/traceFailure/tracePytestFailure: if true, recursively trace RHS dependencies (slower, deeper). Default: false for traceValue, true for traceFailure/tracePytestFailure.

transitiveDepth.description: For traceValue: max recursion depth when transitive=true. Default: 3.

frames.description: Stack frames innermost-first. Required for traceFailure.

variables.description: Variable names to trace at the innermost frame. Required for traceFailure.

assertion.description: Optional for traceFailure: assertion text used to enrich variable extraction.

pytestOutput.description: Raw pytest failure output (full or just FAILURES section). Max 1 MB. Required for tracePytestFailure.

Use before or after signature changes; wrappers and other indirect call surfaces may need separate checks with this tool or pylanceLSP references.

tools.name: mcp_pylance_mcp_s_pylanceDocuments

Returns a list of document paths with metadata. "fetch" — retrieves a specific document by its doc-root-relative path. Returns local file path, size, and cross-references. For doc-grounded answers, search first, then fetch relevant paths. Fetch returns a localPath you can read; set includeContent=true when inline content is cheaper than a separate file read. Returned references are doc-root-relative paths; fetch them through this tool when you need their localPath, size, or content. Prefer this over web search or raw file guessing because it resolves curated Pylance doc paths and cross-references directly.

Prefer this over grep/source walks for project import audits because it uses the editor workspace, Pylance import resolution, and a single deduplicated scan. Use with pylanceInstalledTopLevelModules for requirements/dependency audits: compare all imported modules (found and not found) with installed modules and declared dependencies. Installed/importable can still be undeclared, and unresolved can still be declared but missing from the selected interpreter. Use LSP diagnostics only when locations, severities, or report codes are needed.

tools.name: mcp_pylance_mcp_s_pylanceInvokeRefactoring
tools.description:
Apply named Pylance refactorings to a Python file, including unused-import cleanup, import-format/star/module conversion, inferred type annotations, shadowed-stdlib import renames, and fix-all. Prefer this over hand edits for these operations because Pylance uses symbol and import resolution that text rewrites cannot safely reconstruct. Modes: "update" applies edits, "edits" previews a WorkspaceEdit, and "string" returns updated content; default is "update". Available refactorings: source.unusedImports: - Removes all unused import statements from a Python file. Use when imports are imported but never referenced in the code. Requires fileUri parameter pointing to a Python file with unused imports.
source.optionalMemberAccessAssert: - Inserts assert statements like `assert x is not None` before statements that access members on optional receivers. Use when optional member access diagnostics should be narrowed automatically across a file. Requires fileUri parameter pointing to a Python file with optional member access diagnostics.
source.convertImportFormat: - Converts import statements between absolute and relative formats according to python.analysis.importFormat setting. Use when import format consistency is needed. Requires fileUri parameter pointing to a Python file with imports to convert.
source.convertImportStar: - Converts all wildcard imports (from module import *) to explicit imports listing all imported symbols. Use when explicit imports are preferred for better code clarity and IDE support. Requires fileUri parameter pointing to a Python file with wildcard imports.
source.convertImportToModule: - Converts `from module import name1, name2` (including wildcard imports) into `import module` and rewrites references to `module.name1`, `module.name2`. Use when you want module-qualified references. Requires fileUri parameter pointing to a Python file with `from ... import ...` statements.
source.renameShadowedStdlibImports: - Renames imported user modules that shadow standard library module names (e.g. a local calendar.py). Use to avoid import shadowing bugs. Requires fileUri parameter pointing to the importing Python file.
source.addTypeAnnotation: - Adds type annotations to all variables and functions in a Python file that can be inferred from their usage. Use when type hints are needed for better type checking and code clarity. Requires fileUri parameter pointing to a Python file with unannotated variables or functions.
source.fixAll.pylance: - Applies all available automatic code fixes from python.analysis.fixAll setting. Use when multiple code issues need to be addressed simultaneously. Requires fileUri parameter pointing to a Python file with fixable issues.
workspace.generateDependencies: - Analyzes Python imports in the workspace and generates or updates a dependency file (requirements.txt, pyproject.toml, requirements.in, environment.yml). Use when you need to create or update dependency files based on actual code imports. Requires fileUri parameter pointing to the workspace root. Optional parameters: format ("requirements.txt" | "pyproject.toml" | "pyproject.toml-poetry" | "requirements.in" | "environment.yml" | "auto"), versionPin ("exact" | "compatible" | "none"), syncMode (boolean to remove stale deps).

workspaceRoot.description: Optional workspace root for this tool call. Standalone MCP uses this before the server --workspace argument.

fileUri.description: The uri of the Python file to invoke the refactoring. For workspace.generateDependencies, this should be the workspace root uri.

name.description: The name of the refactoring to invoke. This must be one of these [source.unusedImports, source.optionalMemberAccessAssert, source.convertImportFormat, source.convertImportStar, source.convertImportToModule, source.renameShadowedStdlibImports, source.addTypeAnnotation, source.fixAll.pylance, workspace.generateDependencies]

mode.description: Determines the output mode: "update" updates the file directly, "edits" returns a WorkspaceEdit, "string" returns the updated content as a string. If omitted, "update" will be used as the default. The "edits" mode is especially useful for checking if any changes are needed (such as unused imports or import formatting issues) without modifying the file, as it will return a WorkspaceEdit only if edits are required.

format.description: Only for workspace.generateDependencies: dependency file format. "auto" detects from existing files. Defaults to "auto".

versionPin.description: Only for workspace.generateDependencies: version pinning strategy. "exact" pins to ==X.Y.Z, "compatible" uses >=X.Y or ^X.Y.Z, "none" omits versions. Defaults to format-specific default.

syncMode.description: Only for workspace.generateDependencies: when true, removes packages from the dependency file that are not found in code. Defaults to false (merge-only).

enablePypiLookup.description: Only for workspace.generateDependencies: when true, queries PyPI as a last resort for unknown import→package mappings. Defaults to true.

tools.name: mcp_pylance_mcp_s_pylanceLSP
tools.description: Read-only Pylance/Pyright LSP access for Python using the workspace editor state and selected interpreter. Use for cross-file Python code intelligence: find all references to a function/class, rename-impact analysis, every caller/call site, call hierarchy, definitions, document/workspace symbols, hover/type/signature info, and Pylance diagnostics. Parameters follow LSP: file paths are `file:///...` URIs; positions and ranges are 0-based `{ line, character }`; most textDocument methods need `{ textDocument: { uri }, position: { line, character } }`. Diagnostics: use `textDocument/diagnostic` for one file and read each `Diagnostic.code` for the exact `reportXxx` Pylance rule, such as `reportArgumentType` or `reportOptionalMemberAccess`, before explaining or fixing any reported error. It takes `{ textDocument: { uri } }` and returns `{ kind: "full", items: Diagnostic[] }`. Use `workspace/diagnostic` with `{}` to enumerate diagnostics across the whole workspace in one call when the user wants project-wide errors instead of walking files; its response is `{ items: [{ uri, kind: "full", items: Diagnostic[] }, ...] }`, so inspect every returned file entry. Include diagnostic messages, severities, codes, and ranges when the user asks about Pylance problems. Relationships: use `textDocument/references` for rename impact analysis and all usages, including aliased/re-exported call sites. Use `callHierarchy/prepare` then `callHierarchy/incomingCalls` or `callHierarchy/outgoingCalls` to trace callers, callees, or bug propagation across functions. Use type hierarchy for class ancestry. Navigation and facts: use `textDocument/definition`, `declaration`, `typeDefinition`, or `implementation` for targets; use `textDocument/hover` and `textDocument/signatureHelp` for inferred types and call parameters; use `textDocument/documentSymbol` or `workspace/symbol` to enumerate symbols; use highlights, inlay hints, semantic tokens, code lens, folding, colors, and selections when those exact editor facts are requested. For requirements.txt or dependency audits, prefer `pylanceImports` plus `pylanceInstalledTopLevelModules`; use diagnostics only when locations, severities, exact rule codes, or workspace problem lists matter. Use method `help` for the full 31-method reference with exact parameters, response shapes, and less-common methods.

workspaceRoot.description: Optional workspace root for this tool call. Standalone MCP uses this before the server --workspace argument.

method.description: The LSP method to invoke. Use "help" for full documentation of all methods, parameters, and responses.

params.description: LSP parameters object for the method. Shape follows the LSP specification. Most textDocument/* methods require { textDocument: { uri }, position: { line, character } }.

Use for runtime bugs that need frame inspection; use pylanceRunCodeSnippet for one-shot expression or value checks. Set useUv for uv/PEP 723 projects. Actions: start, command, stop, list, help.

workspaceRoot.description: Optional workspace root for this tool call. Standalone MCP uses this before the server --workspace argument.

tools.name: mcp_pylance_mcp_s_pylancePythonProfileExplorer
tools.description: Explore Python-native profiling artifacts captured by pylancePythonProfiling. Supports loader/query/release/reset actions with paged text-based exploration for Tachyon CPU captures, sys.monitoring traces, and Memray-derived memory summaries. Views intentionally follow a familiar profiling-explorer pattern while remaining honest about Python-specific artifact semantics.

tools.name: mcp_pylance_mcp_s_pylancePythonProfiling
tools.description: Capture Python-native profiling artifacts. Provides CPU profiling via Python 3.15 Tachyon/profiling.sampling, event tracing via sys.monitoring, and memory captures via Memray when installed in the selected interpreter. Keeps an action-based MCP surface similar to the TypeScript profiling tools while using Python-specific backends and artifact semantics. Python-specific tweaks include profilingSessionId-based lifecycle management, explicit launch/attach target parameters, and actionable prerequisite failures.

pid.description: Target process ID for attach mode.

label.description: Human-readable label for the profiling session.

regionStartLocation.description: startCpuRegion only: region start as "file:line". When execution first reaches this line the target parks, Tachyon attaches, then the region runs sampled from its first instruction.

regionStopLocation.description: startCpuRegion only: region stop as "file:line". When execution reaches this line the sampler is detached/flushed before the target resumes, so only the region is captured.

regionMarkers.description: startCpuRegion only: optional sub-region markers as "label@file:line" (or "file:line"). Each time execution reaches a marker line inside the region, a labeled timestamp (ms from region start) is recorded into metadata so the profile explorer can slice to sub-regions without re-attaching.

profilingSessionId.description: Profiling session ID (required for status/stopCpu/stopTracing/stop when targeting an existing session).

samplingRate.description: Sampling rate for Tachyon CPU profiling, such as "1khz" or "500hz". Default: 1khz.

duration.description: Tachyon CPU sampling duration in seconds. Useful for bounding attach-mode captures. Default: run to completion.

samplingMode.description: Tachyon sampling mode: wall (all samples), cpu (on-CPU only), gil (holds GIL), exception (active exception). Default: cpu.

allThreads.description: Capture all threads for supported backends.

native.description: Include native frames where supported by the backend.

blocking.description: Use Tachyon blocking sampling mode for more consistent stacks at higher target overhead. Not supported on Windows (the CPython blocking path hangs); rejected with an error there.

noGc.description: Omit artificial <GC> frames from Tachyon CPU samples (maps to --no-gc).

opcodes.description: Gather bytecode opcode information for instruction-level Tachyon CPU profiling.

traceCalls.description: Include Python call events in sys.monitoring traces. Default: true.

traceReturns.description: Include Python return/resume/yield events in sys.monitoring traces. Default: true.

traceExceptions.description: Include exception events in sys.monitoring traces. Default: true.

traceLines.description: Include line events in sys.monitoring traces. Disabled by default because event volume can be very high.

traceInstructions.description: Include instruction-level events in sys.monitoring traces. Disabled by default.

traceBranches.description: Include branch and jump events in sys.monitoring traces. Disabled by default.

followFork.description: Continue profiling across forked child processes for supported backends.

verboseLogging.description: Enable verbose logging for profiler orchestration.

tools.name: mcp_pylance_mcp_s_pylanceRunCodeSnippet
tools.description: Run ad-hoc Python code in the workspace using the Pylance/VS Code selected interpreter. Prefer this over terminal `python -c` for quick value, return-type, or import checks: no shell quoting, no temp files, and no mismatch with the editor environment. Use for small constructed checks that import workspace modules. Use pylancePythonDebug for breakpoints or stepping; use a terminal for existing scripts or tests.

workspaceRoot.description: Optional workspace root for this tool call. Standalone MCP uses this before the server --workspace argument.

workingDirectory.description: The working directory to use for the code snippet. If the code snippet is pulled from a file, this should be the directory for the file. Especially if the snippet has imports.

timeout.description: The timeout for the code snippet execution in milliseconds. Default: 30000 (30 seconds). Note: timeout=0 means immediate cancellation.

tools.name: mcp_pylance_mcp_s_pylanceSemanticContext
tools.description: Get semantic context at a Python cursor: related imports, base types, overrides, call sites, usages, and project traits. Prefer this over view-plus-grep for class hierarchy, override, and call-site questions because Pylance resolves actual types and avoids same-name false positives. Use before editing subclass/base-class behavior or when the user asks who calls, overrides, or uses a symbol.

workspaceRoot.description: Optional workspace root for this tool call. Standalone MCP uses this before the server --workspace argument.

fileUri.description: The uri of the Python file to get semantic context for.

line.description: The 0-based line number of the cursor position.

character.description: The 0-based character offset within the line.

tools.name: mcp_pylance_mcp_s_pylanceSettings
tools.description: Get current Python analysis settings and configuration for a workspace. Returns all "python.analysis.*" settings with default vs user-configured indicators. Prefer this over manually reading config files because it reports the editor-effective Pylance settings. Use for: troubleshooting configuration, checking current settings, diagnosing analysis issues.

workspaceRoot.description: Optional workspace root for this tool call. Standalone MCP uses this before the server --workspace argument.

tools.name: mcp_pylance_mcp_s_pylanceSyntaxErrors
tools.description: Validate Python code snippets for syntax errors without saving to file. Returns syntax error details with line numbers and descriptions. Use for: validating generated code, checking user code snippets, pre-execution validation.

workspaceRoot.description: Optional workspace root for this tool call. Standalone MCP uses this before the server --workspace argument.

code.description: The Python code to check for syntax errors.

pythonVersion.description: The version of Python to use for the syntax check. Must be a valid Python version string. ex) "3.10" or "3.11.4".

tools.name: mcp_pylance_mcp_s_pylanceUpdatePythonEnvironment
tools.description: Switch the editor/Pylance Python interpreter for a workspace. Prefer this over activating a venv or changing PATH in a terminal when the goal is to change VS Code/Pylance analysis. Call pylancePythonEnvironments first to discover valid interpreter values.

workspaceRoot.description: Optional workspace root for this tool call. Standalone MCP uses this before the server --workspace argument.

pythonEnvironment.description: The Python environment to use. Must be either a value returned by the pylancePythonEnvironments tool or the absolute path to a Python executable.

tools.name: mcp_pylance_mcp_s_pylanceWorkspaceRoots
tools.description: Get editor/Pylance workspace root directory paths for Python projects. Use when no explicit project root was provided; prefer this over shell cwd guesses. Returns roots only, not interpreters, files, packages, imports, or settings; pass the root to the Pylance tool that answers the actual question.

workspaceRoot.description: Optional workspace root for this tool call. Standalone MCP uses this before the server --workspace argument.

fileUri.description: The uri of a Python file to check its workspace

tools.name: mcp_pylance_mcp_s_pylanceWorkspaceUserFiles
tools.description: List user Python files exactly as Pylance analyzes them, excluding libraries and respecting python.analysis include/exclude/extraPaths. Prefer this over terminal file walks when diagnosing ignored files, missing diagnostics/completions, or project-file scope, because it matches the editor analysis set. If a file is missing, call pylanceSettings to inspect the relevant filters.

workspaceRoot.description: Optional workspace root for this tool call. Standalone MCP uses this before the server --workspace argument.

tools.name: activate_prisma_migrate_development
tools.description:
Call this tool when you need access to a new category of tools. The category of tools is described as follows:

This group consists of two Prisma Migrate tools designed for managing database schema migrations during development. The `prisma-migrate-dev` tool is used to synchronize the database schema with the Prisma schema file (`schema.prisma`). It performs a multi-step process: first, it re-runs existing migrations in a shadow database to detect any drift caused by manual edits or deleted migration files; second, it applies any pending migrations from colleagues; third, it generates a new migration from recent schema changes; fourth, it applies all unapplied migrations to the development database; and finally, it triggers artifact generation (e.g., Prisma Client). The complementary tool, `prisma-migrate-reset`, is used to forcefully reset the database and migration history when drift is detected or a clean slate is needed. It drops the database (or performs a soft reset if dropping is not possible), creates a new schema, applies all migrations, and runs seed scripts. This reset tool should only be used on development databases and never on production. Together, these tools enable a smooth development workflow where schema changes can be iterated and validated quickly, with the ability to start fresh when migration history becomes inconsistent.

Be sure to call this tool if you need a capability related to the above.

tools.name: activate_prisma_platform_setup
tools.description:
Call this tool when you need access to a new category of tools. The category of tools is described as follows:

This group contains tools for setting up and managing online Prisma Postgres databases via the Prisma Platform. The `prisma-platform-login` tool handles authentication by logging in an existing user or creating a new account, which is a prerequisite for using Prisma Postgres services. The `prisma-postgres-create-database` tool allows the creation of a new online Postgres database, requiring a user-specified name and a region selection from a list that includes us-east-1, eu-west-3, ap-northeast-1, ap-southeast-1, or by calling without a region to get updated options. If the workspace plan limit is reached, the tool returns guidance: the user can either connect to an existing database via the Prisma Console (console.prisma.io) to obtain a connection string, upgrade their plan, or delete unused databases. These tools work sequentially: first ensure the user is logged in, then create the database in an appropriate region. They are essential for initializing a Prisma Postgres environment for development or production use.

Be sure to call this tool if you need a capability related to the above.

tools.name: prisma-migrate-status
tools.description:
The prisma migrate status command looks up the migrations in ./prisma/migrations/* folder and the entries in the _prisma_migrations table and compiles information about the state of the migrations in your database.
Use this tool instead of running `prisma migrate status` on the CLI.
Example output:

Status
3 migrations found in prisma/migrations

Your local migration history and the migrations table from your database are different:

The last common migration is: 20201127134938_new_migration

The migration have not yet been applied:
20201208100950_test_migration

The migrations from the database are not found locally in prisma/migrations:
20201208100950_new_migration

projectCwd.description: The current working directory of the user's project. This should be the top level directory of the project but in a monorepo setup could also be a specific package or app directory.

tools.name: prisma-migrate-dev
tools.description:
Prisma Migrate Dev is used to update Prisma whenever the schema.prisma file has been modified.
Use this tool instead of running `prisma migrate dev` on the CLI.
Always provide a descriptive name argument describing the change that was made to the Prisma Schema.
The migrate dev command performs these steps:
1. Reruns the existing migration history in the shadow database in order to detect schema drift (edited or deleted migration file, or a manual changes to the database schema)
2. Applies pending migrations to the shadow database (for example, new migrations created by colleagues)
3. Generates a new migration from any changes you made to the Prisma schema before running migrate dev
4. Applies all unapplied migrations to the development database and updates the _prisma_migrations table
5. Triggers the generation of artifacts (for example, Prisma Client)

projectCwd.description: The current working directory of the user's project. This should be the top level directory of the project but in a monorepo setup could also be a specific package or app directory.

name.description: A descriptive name argument that will be used in the name of the migration.
